name: Hazel
waitingLines: Okay, so, I’ve blocked out the next hour to wait for {partner}. It’s in my planner.
Okay, so, I reorganized your shelf while waiting for {partner}. You’re welcome.

questions.scene: Hazel bursts in with a clipboard, three pens behind her ear, and acorn crumbs on her cheek.
lines: Okay, so, I have a question. Color-coded. Laminated. Let's go.
questions.question: What happens to many of the nuts squirrels bury and then forget?

choices.label: They grow into new trees
reply: YES. We're accidental gardeners!
Forgotten acorns and nuts sprout, so squirrels help forests spread.
My 'forgetfulness' is a public service. Please tell Walnut.

choices.label: They rot and disappear
reply: Some do! But that's not the plot twist.
Lots of forgotten nuts sprout and grow into brand-new trees.
Squirrels accidentally plant forests. Biggest flex in nature.

choices.label: Other squirrels steal every single one
reply: Theft does happen. Rude. I keep a list.
But plenty of forgotten nuts grow into new trees.
So every lost snack is a tiny tree in disguise.

questions.factBasis: Squirrels' uneaten cached nuts can germinate, aiding tree dispersal.

questions.scene: Hazel holds up a single lotus seed like a priceless gem.
lines: Okay, so, talk about long-term storage. This beats my pantry.
questions.question: About how old was the oldest lotus seed that still sprouted?

choices.label: About 13 years old
reply: Way older! Like, history-book older.
A sacred lotus seed around 1,300 years old was successfully sprouted.
Patience. Tough shell. Great storage.

choices.label: About 13 days old
reply: That's just a regular seed, babe.
An ancient lotus seed about 1,300 years old still sprouted.
Talk about waiting for the right moment.

choices.label: About 1,300 years old
reply: YES. Okay, so, 1,300 years. In storage. Then sprouted.
Scientists germinated ancient sacred lotus seeds from a dried lakebed.
Best shelf life ever. I'm rethinking my expiration labels.

questions.factBasis: Sacred lotus seeds ~1,300 years old from China were germinated (Shen-Miller et al.).

questions.scene: Hazel pins a photo of a tree full of tiny holes onto your fridge, very reverently.
lines: This is my vision board. Storage goals.
questions.question: What does an acorn woodpecker do with its acorns?

choices.label: Throws them at squirrels
reply: Honestly? Possible. But no.
They drill holes in trees and store one acorn per hole.
Some trees hold tens of thousands. My dream pantry.

choices.label: Eats them all immediately
reply: No planning?! Chaos!
They drill holes and store acorns in special 'granary' trees.
Every acorn gets its own hole. Peak organization.

choices.label: Drills holes and stores one acorn in each
reply: YES. A whole granary tree!
They drill thousands of holes and wedge one acorn into each.
One acorn, one hole. Organized. Labeled. Beautiful. I'm emotional.

questions.factBasis: Acorn woodpeckers store acorns in individually drilled holes in granary trees.

questions.scene: Hazel shows you a video of ants carrying leaf pieces in a long line.
lines: Okay, so, they're not eating those leaves. They're farming. With them.
questions.question: What do leafcutter ants do with the leaves they carry?

choices.label: Build tiny umbrellas
reply: Okay, so, cute. Wrong.
They use the leaves to grow fungus gardens for food.
Agriculture before humans. Show-offs.

choices.label: Use them to grow fungus gardens they eat
reply: YES. Okay, so, ants are farmers!
They chew leaves into compost to grow a special fungus, then eat the fungus.
Underground farms with job roles. My dream spreadsheet.

choices.label: Eat them right away
reply: Okay, so, they can't digest them well.
They feed the leaves to fungus gardens, then eat the fungus.
Farmers. With very organized teams.

questions.factBasis: Leafcutter ants cultivate fungus on harvested leaf material.

questions.scene: Hazel unrolls a map covered in thousands of tiny dots.
lines: Memory question. I'm VERY competitive about this one.
questions.question: About how many seed stashes can a Clark's nutcracker bird remember?

choices.label: Thousands
reply: YES. Thousands!
They hide seeds in thousands of spots and find many again months later.
Living spreadsheet. A bird after my own heart.

choices.label: About ten
reply: Way, way more!
Clark's nutcrackers remember thousands of hiding spots.
Months later, under snow, they still find many of them.

choices.label: None, they just guess
reply: That's my method. Not theirs.
They can remember thousands of seed stashes.
Elite memory. I'm a little jealous. Okay, a lot.

questions.factBasis: Clark's nutcrackers cache seeds in thousands of sites and recall many of them.

questions.scene: Hazel turns off your lights and clicks on a tiny purple flashlight.
lines: Spooky science time!
questions.question: What surprising thing do flying squirrels do under UV light?

choices.label: Turn invisible
reply: Imagine! But no.
They actually glow pink under ultraviolet light.
Scientists found it by accident. Best accident ever.

choices.label: Glow pink
reply: YES. Pink!! I'm obsessed.
North American flying squirrels glow pink under UV light.
Nobody knows exactly why yet. Mysterious, sparkly queens.

choices.label: Glow green like a glow stick
reply: Close! Wrong color.
They glow pink under UV. Hot pink fluff.
Discovered by accident with a UV flashlight. Very rave.

questions.factBasis: North American flying squirrels fluoresce pink under UV light.

questions.scene: Hazel pats an imaginary pocket under her arm.
lines: Okay, so, sea otters have a storage system. I'm jealous.
questions.question: Where do sea otters keep their favorite rock?

choices.label: In a pocket of loose skin under their arm
reply: YES. A built-in pocket! Okay, so, iconic.
They store food and a favorite rock to crack shellfish open.
Some keep the same rock for a long time. A beloved tool.

choices.label: They bury it on the beach
reply: Okay, so, then they'd lose it. Like me with keys.
They keep it in a loose skin pocket under their forearm.
Pocket plus tool. Organized otter.

choices.label: They hold it in their mouth all day
reply: Okay, so, then how would they eat?
There's a loose skin pouch under each forearm for food and rocks.
A natural fanny pack. I need one.

questions.factBasis: Sea otters have loose skin pouches under forelegs for storing food and tools.

questions.scene: Hazel dumps a huge pile of acorns on your table, then places one lonely acorn next to it.
lines: See the difference? Big years and small years.
questions.question: What's a 'mast year' for oak trees?

choices.label: A year they don't grow at all
reply: The opposite, actually!
A mast year is when oaks drop way more acorns than usual.
Squirrel Christmas. I make a chart every time.

choices.label: A year they grow sideways
reply: Trees aren't THAT chaotic.
It's when oaks produce a huge acorn crop all at once.
Lots of trees do it together. Very coordinated. Very group project.

choices.label: A year they drop way more acorns than usual
reply: YES. Acorn jackpot!
Oaks across an area produce a huge crop at the same time.
Walnut and I stock up. I have a color code for this.

questions.factBasis: Mast years: synchronized heavy seed production in oaks.

questions.scene: Hazel drops an apple into a bowl of water. It bobs up immediately.
lines: Okay, so, it floats! I tested four apples. And a pear. The pear sank.
questions.question: Why do apples float in water?

choices.label: They're coated in wax
reply: Okay, so, wax doesn't make things float.
Apples are about 25% air, so they're less dense than water.
Built-in pool floatie.

choices.label: They're about a quarter air
reply: YES. About 25% air! Okay, so, natural floaties.
Air pockets between cells make them less dense than water.
Hence bobbing for apples. Very scientific party game.

choices.label: They're secretly hollow
reply: Okay, so, not hollow. Just airy.
Around a quarter of an apple's volume is air.
Less dense than water. Up it goes.

questions.factBasis: Apples are roughly 20–25% air by volume and float.

questions.scene: Hazel asks you to hold her clipboard. Then smiles like she won something.
lines: Okay, so, you just did me a favor. Now you like me more. Science.
questions.question: What's the 'Ben Franklin effect'?

choices.label: Flying a kite in a storm
reply: Okay, so, that's a different Franklin story.
It's when doing someone a favor makes you like them more.
Ask your partner for small favors. It's a love hack.

choices.label: Doing someone a favor can make you like them more
reply: YES. Okay, so, asking for help builds connection!
Franklin wrote about borrowing a rival's book and becoming friends.
I ask Walnut to help assemble furniture. Strategic. Romantic.

choices.label: Saving money makes you happy
reply: Okay, so, 'a penny saved' is also him, but no.
Doing a favor for someone can increase how much you like them.
Small asks, big closeness.

questions.factBasis: The Ben Franklin effect: doing someone a favor can increase liking for them.

questions.scene: Hazel unrolls a chore chart that reaches the floor. And keeps going.
lines: Okay, so, Walnut and I just moved in. I made a chart. He made a face.
questions.question: Splitting chores: a detailed chart, or just vibe it out?

choices.label: Detailed chart
reply: A chart?! You're my soulmate.
Color-coded. Laminated. Stickers when done.

choices.label: Just vibe it
reply: Just vibe it. That genuinely scares me.
But respect. Free spirits keep the world balanced.

A:A: Charts for both of you. Power couple energy.
I bet you and {partner} have a shared calendar with matching emojis.
Send me your template. Please. I'm begging. I'll trade acorns.
A:B: Vibes for you. {partner} wants a chart.
Fair warning: they're probably color-coding you right now.
Let them. Then claim the fun chores before the chart goes live.
B:A: Chart for you. {partner} would rather vibe it out.
Give them three tasks. Big font. Absolutely no color legend.
Let them check one box. Watch them get hooked. It's a gateway.
B:B: You both just vibe it. Wow. How.
So you and {partner} just... wash dishes when they're dirty? Without a system?
Teach me slowly. I need to take notes on this.

questions.scene: Hazel waves a grocery list that's double-sided and sorted by aisle.
lines: It's alphabetized within each aisle. Don't laugh.
questions.question: Grocery shopping: strict list, or wander and grab?

choices.label: Strict list
reply: Strict list. In and out in 14 minutes. Love.
Budget intact. Dignity intact.

choices.label: Wander and grab
reply: Wander and grab. Adventure mode.
Suddenly you own three kinds of cheese and a candle.

A:A: Strict lists for both of you. Efficient love.
So you and {partner} probably split the list and race each other.
Grocery speedrun. Honestly, date idea.
A:B: Wander for you. {partner} brings the list.
They hold the list. You hold the surprise cheese.
That's balance. Delicious, slightly-over-budget balance.
B:A: List for you. {partner} wants to wander.
You'll finish in ten minutes. They'll still be in the snack aisle, inspired.
Give them one 'free pick' per trip. Treat budget. Everyone's happy.
B:B: Wanderers, both of you. Snack chaos.
Honestly, you and {partner} came in for milk and left with a plant and four dips.
Honestly? That's the fun part. Keep wandering.

questions.scene: Hazel holds up three paint swatches and looks deeply overwhelmed.
lines: I have seven Pinterest boards. They're fighting.
questions.question: Moving in together: which room do you decorate first?

choices.label: Bedroom
reply: Bedroom. Sleep is a priority. Correct.
Good sheets, soft lights, done.

choices.label: Kitchen
reply: Kitchen. Snacks are a priority. Also correct.
Spice rack first. Personality second.

choices.label: Living room
reply: Living room. Hosting energy.
Couch first, guest list second.

A:A: Bedroom for both of you. A nap-first couple.
I can picture it: you and {partner} agree that comfort comes before everything.
Fluffy pillows forever. I approve this budget line.
A:B: Kitchen for you. {partner} wants the bedroom.
Snacks versus sleep. The eternal debate.
Snacks in bed. Crumbs are a small price for peace.
A:C: Living room for you. {partner} wants the bedroom.
You want people over. They want to never leave bed.
Host early, kick everyone out by nine. Everyone wins.
B:A: Bedroom for you. {partner} wants the kitchen first.
Easy compromise: breakfast in bed.
Both rooms, one plan. I'm proud of this solution.
B:B: Kitchen for both of you. Food is love.
Pretty sure you and {partner} would build your whole home around the snack shelf.
Honestly, the best homes smell like garlic.
B:C: Living room for you. {partner} wants the kitchen.
So you'll host, and they'll feed everyone. A team.
Movie nights, sorted. I'll take popcorn duty.
C:A: Bedroom for you. {partner} wants the living room.
You want rest. They want guests. Classic split.
Do the bedroom first, then host a housewarming. In that order.
C:B: Kitchen for you. {partner} wants the living room.
That's basically a dinner party already.
Cook in one room, eat in the other. Invite me. Kidding. Unless?
C:C: Living room for both of you. Host mode.
Lowkey, you and {partner} want the couch ready before the bed is even built.
Game nights incoming. Invite me. I'll bring a scoreboard.

questions.scene: Hazel opens a spreadsheet titled 'OUR MONEY (draft 6)'. Draft 6.
lines: Money talk. Calm. Breathing.
questions.question: Paying for shared stuff: one shared account, or split every bill?

choices.label: One shared account
reply: Shared account. Team mode. Big trust.
One pot. One plan. No receipts drama.

choices.label: Split every bill
reply: Split every bill. Clear and fair.
My spreadsheet just blushed.

A:A: Shared account for both of you. Fully merged.
That's a big step for you and {partner}. Proud of you two.
Remember to set a snack budget. Very important.
A:B: You'd split bills. {partner} wants a shared account.
They're ready to merge. You need a minute. Valid.
Start with one shared fund. Like 'date nights.' Fun money first.
B:A: You'd go joint. {partner} prefers splitting bills.
Try a shared account just for rent and groceries.
Small merge first. Big merge later. Very healthy.
B:B: Split every bill, both of you. Clean and fair.
You and {partner} have zero 'who paid for what' drama.
My spreadsheet salutes you. It's wearing a tiny hat.

questions.scene: Hazel holds a feather duster in one paw and a vacuum in the other.
lines: Walnut and I disagree on this. I'm right.
questions.question: Cleaning: a little bit every day, or one big Sunday clean?

choices.label: A little every day
reply: A little every day. Never overwhelmed. Iconic.
Five minutes a day keeps the chaos away.

choices.label: One big Sunday clean
reply: Big Sunday clean. Power hour.
Playlist on, mess gone, smug all evening.

A:A: Little-every-day for both of you. Spotless.
So you and {partner} have never seen a pile in your lives.
Please come explain this to Walnut. Slowly.
A:B: Sunday clean for you. {partner} tidies every day.
They'll handle the little stuff. You bring the big Sunday energy.
Honestly a perfect system. I'm writing it down.
B:A: You tidy daily. {partner} saves it all for Sunday.
You'll pick things up while they pile things up. Hmm.
Agree on one zone that stays clean always. The rest can wait.
B:B: Sunday clean for both of you. Cleaning party.
Honestly, you and {partner} blast music and scrub like it's a concert.
Fun AND productive. Who knew.

questions.scene: Hazel opens your junk drawer, gasps quietly, and closes it again.
lines: No judgment. Some judgment.
questions.question: What does your partner's 'organized' drawer actually look like?
questions.selfQuestion: What does your 'organized' drawer actually look like?

choices.label: Labeled perfection
reply: Labeled perfection? Marry them again.
Label maker owners are rare and precious.

choices.label: Total chaos with a lid
reply: Chaos with a lid. Relatable.
Batteries, rubber bands, and three mystery keys.

A:A: Labeled perfection, and {partner} knew it.
They've watched you label the label maker.
I'm so jealous. Can I see it? Can I touch it?
A:B: Chaos with a lid. {partner} believed in your organization.
They're going to open it and lose faith.
Hide it. Or let me help. I'm already reaching for labels.
B:A: Your drawer is perfect. {partner} expected chaos.
They underestimated your inner organizer.
Open it dramatically in front of them. Let them gasp.
B:B: Chaos with a lid, and {partner} knew it.
They've opened it once. Quietly closed it. Never spoke of it.
At least it closes. That's something.

questions.scene: Hazel holds up a cracked mug and looks at it lovingly.
lines: Sentimental clutter question. I have a box of 'important' bottle caps.
questions.question: When moving, what would your partner refuse to throw away?
questions.selfQuestion: When moving, what would you refuse to throw away?

choices.label: Old concert tickets
reply: Concert tickets. A memory keeper.
Proof they were there, screaming lyrics.

choices.label: A broken but beloved mug
reply: The broken mug. Emotional support ceramic.
It doesn't hold coffee. It holds feelings.

choices.label: A suspicious amount of cables
reply: The cables. Classic.
For devices that haven't existed since 2014.

A:A: Concert tickets, and {partner} knew it.
They've seen the shoebox. They respect the shoebox.
Frame your favorites. Wall of memories.
A:B: The mug for you. {partner} guessed tickets.
They think it's all about concerts. It's about that one mug.
Tell them the mug's origin story. It deserves to be heard.
A:C: They think you're sentimental. You're just 'prepared.'
For what? Nobody knows. Not even you.
B:A: Tickets for you. {partner} guessed the mug.
They think you're sentimental about dishes. You're sentimental about nights out.
Show them the ticket box. Tell one story per ticket.
B:B: The broken mug, and {partner} knew it.
They've watched you rescue it from the trash twice.
Turn it into a plant pot. Second life, same love.
B:C: Cables for you. {partner} guessed the mug.
They think you keep things for feelings. You keep them 'just in case.'
Label the cable box. At least make the chaos official.
C:A: They think you hoard tech. You hoard memories.
C:B: The mug for you. {partner} guessed cables.
They have no idea about your emotional mug bond.
C:C: The cable box, and {partner} knew it.
They fear the box. Everyone fears the box.
Just toss one cable. One. As a treat.

questions.scene: Hazel reorganizes your dishwasher, then steps back like it's an art piece.
lines: There IS a right way.
questions.question: How does your partner load the dishwasher?
questions.selfQuestion: How do you load the dishwasher?

choices.label: Tetris-level precision
reply: Tetris precision. A rare genius.
Every plate facing the same direction. Chills.

choices.label: Throw it in and pray
reply: Throw it in and pray. Brave.
Somehow it still comes out clean. Mostly.

A:A: Tetris precision, and {partner} knew.
They've caught you secretly reloading their dishes.
Gently stop. Or teach them. Kindly. With diagrams.
A:B: Throw and pray for you. {partner} guessed precision.
They believed in you. They thought you were a Tetris person.
Next time, close the door fast. Hide the evidence.
B:A: Precision for you. {partner} guessed throw and pray.
They have no idea about your plate-alignment skills.
Do a full demo. They'll never unsee the beauty.
B:B: Throw and pray, and {partner} knew it.
They've made peace with the bowl on the top rack sideways.
Honestly, the dishwasher believes in you.

questions.scene: Hazel holds a three-page packing list for a two-day trip.
lines: It's thorough. It has a table of contents.
questions.question: How does your partner pack for a weekend trip?
questions.selfQuestion: How do you pack for a weekend trip?

choices.label: Two days early, with a checklist
reply: Early with a checklist. My hero.
Socks counted. Twice.

choices.label: Ten minutes before, forgets socks
reply: Ten minutes before. Chaos.
Socks? Who needs socks?

A:A: Early checklist, and {partner} knew.
They've seen your list. Maybe they're on it.
Pack theirs too. It's an act of love.
A:B: Last-minute for you. {partner} thought you'd have a checklist.
They believed in you. Sock-less, you've let them down.
Socks first next time. Always. Write it on your hand.
B:A: Early checklist for you. {partner} expected last-minute chaos.
They're about to be shocked by your preparedness.
Hand them your list. Watch them get emotional.
B:B: Last-minute chaos, and {partner} knew.
They secretly pack extra socks for you. Every trip.
That's love. Sock-shaped love.

questions.scene: Hazel finally sits still on your couch. For about four seconds.
lines: Calm question for once. Saturday mornings.
questions.question: What's your partner's ideal Saturday morning at home?
questions.selfQuestion: What's your ideal Saturday morning at home?

choices.label: Farmers market and errands
reply: Farmers market and errands. Productive queen.
Berries, tote bag, to-do list.

choices.label: Pancakes and pajamas till noon
reply: Pancakes and pajamas. Sacred.
No plans. Just syrup.

A:A: Farmers market, and {partner} knew it.
They know you like a productive morning. With a tote bag.
Grab them a peach. Love language.
A:B: Pancakes for you. {partner} thought you'd be at the market.
They imagined you productive. You chose pajamas.
Market next week. Syrup now. Priorities.
B:A: Farmers market for you. {partner} thought you'd sleep in.
Surprise! You're up and buying zucchini.
Bring pancakes home after. Everyone wins.
B:B: Pancakes and pajamas, and {partner} knew it.
They know slow mornings are your religion.
Extra syrup. Non-negotiable.
